title: One data foundation: a catalog entry per table with its checks, one entity across four systems through the matching kind, and history read as it was
request: Phase 8 Part G, the owner's pattern 10: tables with owners and checks, the same customer in four systems as one view, reads as of a date.
plan: TableEntry v1 with checks run on the table.
resolve: the systems' records matched by the matching kind and linked into entities.
as_of: no row written after the date, the row valid on it for a history table.
A replica with one customer in four systems.

decisions.decision: Resolve through the matching kind, not a join on a key.
decisions.why: Four systems never share a clean key; the matching kind measures its links on a holdout read once.

decisions.decision: as_of applies both the validity and the written date when both are given.
decisions.why: A backdated correction written later was not known on the date.

change: dclab_core.foundation (Check, TableEntry v1, entry, as_of, resolve); dclab_core.matching.link; dclab_core.replicas.four_systems; dclab_rnd.foundation (FND).

findings.defect: A history row written after the date was returned when it was backdated.
findings.scenario: valid from January, written in July, read as of March: returned.
findings.cause: With valid_from given, the written date was ignored.
findings.fix: Both filters apply when both columns are given.

measurements.name: four systems resolved into one view (seed 0)
measurements.gate: the systems' customers resolve with the pair F1 and its interval, beating the exact rule
measurements.result: pair F1 0.9961 (0.9883 to 1.0), the single best field chosen, beats the exact rule
limits: Invented customers: the e-mail is close to unique, so one field nearly decides; real systems are harder.
The known matches are every pair of the replica's truth.

outcome: A table set gets a catalog of entries with checks, a resolved view of one entity across systems with its measured accuracy, and reads as of a date that never see a later row.
lessons: A point-in-time read needs both clocks: when a fact was valid and when it was written.
risks: The replica's single near-unique field makes the matching easy; a harder replica is open.
